title: Audio-reactive track runner/rhythm game update
author: xavium
selftext:
Thought I'd give you all a bit of an update on how the game is going. I spiked a lot of experimental stuff on the gameplay; from flying, full on 6D flying through gates, "strumming" on the wave bars, lots of different things. What I got from those is that 1: the track is a part of the game's identity. Spent a long time getting the track/ribbon to look and feel good, and generate well. Don't really wanna move that to the scenery and have more of a beat saber clone that's hard to control. 2. autopilot can work as long as the mechanics of "hitting notes" are satisfying enough. it's actually cognitive overload to have to steer, control the ship and hit the right notes at the right time, plus it's a mess of keybinds. frees up a lot of space for adding notes to hit at the right times.

  
so now the ship steers itself, you ride through the music, but you hit different notes. Still working on the presentation but basic strike notes you hit with a pulse (default spacebar), "bank" notes that refer to direction, move the track and ship in that direction by pressing the right arrow/wasd at the right time, and hold notes (hold and release on the beats/at the right time). Didn't want to completely copy DDR and having only directional notes presented issues with the track going a bit spaghetti.

  
now the problem is that those notes \_need\_ to feel good, look clear and in keeping with the style of the game, and be placed on the right parts of songs, at runtime, locally. I was using a great solution opus helped me cook up with a dynamic bayesian network postprocessing the FFT with mel spectograms (or something, i dunno, a lot of this still is way over my head. I'm studying audio analysis for this and learning all I can about it, takes time). This worked really well for a lot of genres, and especially well at songs with a clear distinct beat, but as soon as the music got a little noisy, the confidence quickly dropped and it meant there were songs on hard difficulty with barely any notes being placed. 

  
Then I found a paper from 2014 and they used a 20M parameter model specifically trained for detecting the beats and tempo of a song: perfect. the whole thing is open source and about 80MB, so I introduced this and it only added \~4.2sec on average to analysis. So total analysis of a 4 min song is always under 10 seconds, usually closer to 5 sec. It works fantastically, as you see in the video, a mix of genres and the notes are placed correctly on the right beats. I still use my old method of analysing when the model can't be put onto the GPU and where the model is not confident (and the old method is confident), so it's a blend of the two.

I even took this a step further and added confident chorus/verse detection, where note passages and the mix of notes can be reproduced in certain parts of the song (with slight differences to keep it interesting), and now it's really starting to feel like "playing" the song.

  
Added a tutorial and few other bits that needed doing (settings, keybinds, etc.) and it's starting to feel a bit more like something now. Still got a list of bugfixes, probably another polish pass on the notes themselves, the ship and the ui, then I'll start thinking about player testing. I had a mac build that was working so I'll need to figure out how to port that inference model to mac too. yt-dlp integration has been a lifesaver, typing a song name and just getting it to play within the next 5-10 sec is great, and it's not like youtube is lacking for music. This is of course an experimental feature though and i'm definitely not gonna be shipping yt-dlp lol ;)
